title: Goggle Ai Studio Backtesting
author: Affectionate-Fun-623
selftext: Does Google Ai studio actually give accurate back testing results? Every time i give it a script it shows me profit and profit like I'm about to get rich. but when i test it in other places it make me poor again.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Treat those numbers with a lot of suspicion. A language model doesn't backtest anything by itself. Unless it's actually running your code against real historical data, the "results" can be made up, or at best a rough guess. Even when it does run code, it often does so on synthetic or limited data, with zero costs and with look-ahead mistakes it won't warn you about. That's why it looks great there and falls apart on a real platform.

To trust a backtest, you'd want to run it yourself on data you can inspect, using a proper engine (TradingView's Strategy Tester, Backtrader, vectorbt, or your broker's tool). Then check a handful of trades by hand against the chart, add commission and slippage, and test on a period you didn't use to build the strategy. If the AI's profit vanishes at that point, that's the honest answer.

Also see whether your rules rely on information that wasn't available at the time, like earnings figures or macro releases stamped with the wrong time. Cymetica's EventTrader has point-in-time event data that's useful for that check, but any accurate calendar helps.

If you paste the strategy rules, people here can probably tell you which part is inflating the results.

replies.author: Affectionate-Fun-623
replies.body: I gave different ais my pine script and access to binance live prices. Most ai give decent results looses and wins. But google just makes me rich all the time. Can you give tell me about a decent yet free backtesting platform?

replies.author: Affectionate-Fun-623
replies.body: Also I tell the bots to take fees in to consideration. But I know these aren’t 100 percent accurate. Any way I can test these on Binance since it is my primary broker.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
"Makes me rich all the time" is itself the warning sign. Real strategies have losing stretches, so a tool that never shows one is probably inventing or flattering the results.

For a free and decent option, Freqtrade is the one I'd try since you're on Binance. It's open source, backtests on Binance historical data with fees built in, and has a dry-run mode that trades live prices with fake money. Backtesting.py and vectorbt are good if you'd rather write a bit of Python, and Binance publishes free historical candles at data.binance.vision. If you want to keep your Pine script, TradingView's Strategy Tester works on the free plan, though history and features are limited.

To test on Binance itself, use their testnet (spot and futures), which gives you a simulated account with the real API, so you can check order handling before risking anything. After that, run a tiny live account for a few weeks with the rules frozen and compare the fills to what your backtest assumed.

One thing to be careful with is AI telling you fees are included. Verify it in the actual code: look for the fee percentage, and check a couple of trades by hand. Do you trade spot or futures on Binance?

replies.author: Affectionate-Fun-623
replies.body: thank you man really helpful. Glad your actually sharing some well known tools instead of another self promotion. too many of those are disappointing.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Glad it helped. One tip before you start: write down your rules and what "good enough" looks like before you run the first backtest, so you can't talk yourself into a result afterward. And start with Freqtrade's dry-run mode, since you'll see the gap between backtest and live fills within the first week or two. Good luck, and feel free to post what you find.

replies.body: What do you consider to be an optimum time for forward testing?

replies.author: Affectionate-Fun-623
replies.body: Also what I am currently doing now is feeding the bot real time prices with a binance Api and its running on powershell. Am I doing it right?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
There isn't one ideal length, because it should be set by the number of trades and the market conditions you saw, not by the calendar. As a rough guide, I'd want at least 100 trades as a minimum sanity check and ideally 200 or more, spanning more than one kind of market (a trend, a range, and a sharp move). For a 5-minute structure bot that might be a few weeks. A couple of quiet, one-directional weeks won't tell you much.

Your setup is fine in principle, since checking every minute and deciding on the 5m chart doesn't need tick data. What matters is the plumbing. Act only on closed 5m candles, never the one still forming, or you'll get signals that vanish by the close. Handle API errors, rate limits and reconnects. Save the bot's state to disk so a PowerShell restart doesn't lose track of open positions. Log every decision with the candle data and the reason. And model fills with fees and slippage instead of assuming you get the price you saw.

That's a lot to build by hand, so once you're ready I'd move to a platform like Freqtrade, which already handles candle timing, state, logging, fees and dry-run order simulation. You can keep the same logic and port it.

It's also worth logging whether your trades cluster around big releases like CPI or FOMC, which move crypto hard. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing for tagging those.

Are you running in simulation or with real orders right now?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
It isn't backtesting anything. A chat model reading your script is writing what a backtest result would plausibly look like. It never pulled a bar of price data or filled an order, so of course the story it tells is a happy one, and a real engine running the same code tells a different one.

For a real check, run the script somewhere that executes it against actual prices with fees. That gap is why I built Quantradin, a paper desk where a strategy trades on real prices without risking anything, free, at quantradin.com.

comments.author: Traditional_Pie_8262
comments.body: yeah, that’s usually a sign the backtest assumptions are too optimistic. check slippage, fees, and out-of-sample results
